questions.question: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be a convex set and $f\colon D\to\mathbb{R}$ a convex function. At which points does the continuity theorem for convex functions guarantee that $f$ is continuous?
options: At every point of $D$, including all the boundary points of $D$
At every point of $\operatorname{Int}(D)$, not at points of $\partial D$
Only at the points of $D$ where $f$ is differentiable
At every point of $D$ whenever $D$ is closed and bounded

questions.question: The function $f(x)=|x|$ is convex on $\mathbb{R}$ and has a corner at $0$. What does the continuity theorem for convex functions give at the interior point $0$, and does differentiability hold there?
options: $f$ is continuous and differentiable at $0$, since convexity on an open set gives both
$f$ is discontinuous at $0$, since a corner breaks the continuity of a convex function
$f$ is continuous at $0$, but it is not differentiable there
The theorem does not apply at $0$, since the slope of $f$ jumps there

questions.question: Let $I$ be an open interval and let $f\colon I\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous at every point of $I$. What does the continuity theorem for convex functions let you conclude about convexity of $f$ on $I$?
options: Nothing: continuity on $I$ is necessary for convexity, not sufficient
$f$ is convex on $I$, since the theorem is an equivalence on open sets
$f$ is convex or concave on $I$, since $f$ has no jumps inside $I$
$f$ is convex on $I$ as soon as $f$ is also bounded on $I$

questions.question: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be an open convex set and $f\colon D\to\mathbb{R}$ a concave function. Why is $f$ continuous at every point of $D$?
options: The epigraph of a concave $f$ is convex, so the theorem applies to $f$ itself
It need not be: the theorem is about convex functions, so a concave $f$ may jump
A concave function is the minimum of finitely many affine functions
$-f$ is convex, hence continuous on $D$, and then so is $f=-(-f)$

questions.question: Let $f\colon[0,3]\to\mathbb{R}$ be strictly convex. What can be said about continuity of $f$ at the endpoint $3$?
options: $f$ is continuous at $3$, since strict convexity rules out every jump
$f$ is continuous at $3$, since the point $3$ belongs to the closed set $[0,3]$
$f$ may be discontinuous at $3$, since $3$ is not an interior point
$f$ must be discontinuous at $3$, since strictness forces a jump at an endpoint

questions.question: Let $D=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x\geq0,\ y\geq0\}$, the closed first quadrant, and let $f\colon D\to\mathbb{R}$ be convex. Which subset of $D$ is $\operatorname{Int}(D)$, the set on which the continuity theorem makes $f$ continuous?
options: All of $D$, that is, every $(x,y)$ with $x\geq0$ and $y\geq0$
The set of all $(x,y)$ with $x>0$ and $y>0$
The set of all $(x,y)$ with $x>0$ or $y>0$
All of $D$ except the corner point $(0,0)$

questions.question: Define $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ by $f(x)=-x$ for $x<0$, $f(0)=c$, and $f(x)=x^2$ for $x>0$. For which values of $c$ can $f$ be convex on $\mathbb{R}$?
options: For every $c\geq0$, since a convex function may jump up but not down
For every $c\leq0$, since a lower value at $0$ stays below every chord
For every real $c$, since changing one value never affects convexity
Only for $c=0$, since a jump either way at $0$ breaks convexity

questions.question: Let $f(x)=x^2$ for $-3\leq x\leq0$ and $f(x)=x-1$ for $0<x\leq3$. With $a=-1$, $b=\tfrac{1}{4}$ and $\lambda=\tfrac{1}{5}$ one has $\lambda a+(1-\lambda)b=0$. What is $\lambda f(a)+(1-\lambda)f(b)$, and what does it show?
options: $-\tfrac{2}{5}$, which is below $f(0)=0$, so $f$ is not convex
$\tfrac{1}{4}$, which is above $f(0)=0$, so this chord fits convexity
$-\tfrac{2}{5}$, which is above the right limit $-1$, so this chord fits convexity
$\tfrac{13}{20}$, which is at least $f(0)=0$, so the inequality holds here

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{e}_1=(1,0)$, $\boldsymbol{e}_2=(0,1)$. To prove continuity of a convex $f$ at $\boldsymbol{x}_0=(1,1)$ with $r=\tfrac{1}{2}$, the points $\boldsymbol{x}_0\pm r\boldsymbol{e}_k$ must lie in the domain. Which points are these?

A convex $f$ on $(-1,1)$ has $f(0)=2$, $f(-\tfrac{1}{2})=3$ and $f(\tfrac{1}{2})=5$. With $x_0=0$ and $r=\tfrac{1}{2}$, which bound does the estimate of the continuity theorem give for $|h|<\tfrac{1}{2}$?
A function $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is discontinuous at the point $2$. What follows from the continuity theorem for convex functions?
options: $f$ is not convex on $\mathbb{R}$, but it may still be concave on $\mathbb{R}$
$f$ is not convex on any interval that contains the point $2$
$f$ is convex on $\mathbb{R}$ if it is convex on $(-\infty,2)$ and on $(2,\infty)$
Neither $f$ nor $-f$ is convex on $\mathbb{R}$, so $f$ is not concave on $\mathbb{R}$ either

questions.question: For convex $f$ on convex $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\operatorname{Int}(D)$, pick $r>0$ with $\boldsymbol{x}_0\pm r\boldsymbol{e}_k\in D$ ($\boldsymbol{e}_k$ the standard basis vectors). The continuity estimate holds for $|h_1|+\dots+|h_n|<r$. Why this condition?
options: It makes $\boldsymbol{x}_0+\boldsymbol{h}$ a convex combination of $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ and the points $\boldsymbol{x}_0\pm r\boldsymbol{e}_k$, with weight below $1$ on the outer points
It puts $\boldsymbol{x}_0+\boldsymbol{h}$ in the Euclidean ball of radius $r$ about $\boldsymbol{x}_0$, and that ball lies in $D$ with $f$ at most $M$ on it
It makes $f$ differentiable on the segment from $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ to $\boldsymbol{x}_0+\boldsymbol{h}$, so the mean value theorem bounds the change in $f$
It makes $\boldsymbol{x}_0+\boldsymbol{h}$ the midpoint of two of the points $\boldsymbol{x}_0\pm r\boldsymbol{e}_k$, so convexity bounds $f(\boldsymbol{x}_0+\boldsymbol{h})$ by $M$

questions.question: For convex $f$ and $\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\operatorname{Int}(D)$, the continuity proof first shows $f(\boldsymbol{x}_0+\boldsymbol{h})\leq(1-t)f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)+tM$, with $M$ the largest value of $f$ at $\boldsymbol{x}_0\pm r\boldsymbol{e}_k$ and $t=(|h_1|+\dots+|h_n|)/r$. How is a lower bound for $f(\boldsymbol{x}_0+\boldsymbol{h})$ obtained?
options: Apply the upper bound to $-f$, which turns it into a lower bound for $f$ at $\boldsymbol{x}_0+\boldsymbol{h}$
Use convexity at the midpoint $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ of $\boldsymbol{x}_0\pm\boldsymbol{h}$, then the upper bound at $\boldsymbol{x}_0-\boldsymbol{h}$
Use that $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ minimises $f$ near itself, so that $f(\boldsymbol{x}_0+\boldsymbol{h})\geq f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$
Use the smallest value of $f$ at the points $\boldsymbol{x}_0\pm r\boldsymbol{e}_k$, since $f$ stays above it between them

questions.question: For $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$, $\boldsymbol{x}_0=(-1,0)$, $r=2$, let $M$ be the largest value of $f$ at the four points $\boldsymbol{x}_0\pm r\boldsymbol{e}_k$ ($\boldsymbol{e}_1=(1,0)$, $\boldsymbol{e}_2=(0,1)$). What is the constant $\frac{M-f(\boldsymbol{x}_0)}{r}\sqrt{2}$ of the continuity estimate?
options: $\tfrac{9}{2}\sqrt{2}$

questions.question: Let $f(x)=x^2$ for $0\leq x<3$ and $f(3)=c$, so that $f$ is defined on $[0,3]$. For which values of $c$ is $f$ convex on $[0,3]$?
options: Exactly for $c\geq9$
Only for $c=9$
Exactly for $c\leq9$
Exactly for $c\geq\tfrac{17}{2}$

questions.question: A convex $f$ on $(0,4)$ satisfies, by the continuity estimate at $x_0=2$ with $r=\tfrac{1}{2}$, $|f(2+h)-f(2)|\leq4|h|$ for all $|h|<\tfrac{1}{2}$. What is the largest $\delta$ that this estimate alone justifies for $|x-2|<\delta\Rightarrow|f(x)-f(2)|<3$?
options: $\delta=\tfrac{3}{4}$
$\delta=12$
$\delta=3$
$\delta=\tfrac{1}{2}$

questions.question: A student argues: 'For convex $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, the continuity estimate with $r=1$ gives at each $x_0$ a bound $|f(x_0+h)-f(x_0)|\leq(M-f(x_0))|h|$ for $|h|<1$, with $M=\max\{f(x_0-1),f(x_0+1)\}$, so one constant serves at all $x_0$.' For $f(x)=x^2$, what is wrong with this?
options: Nothing: with $r=1$ the constant $M-f(x_0)$ equals $3$ at every $x_0$
The constant $M-f(x_0)=2|x_0|+1$ depends on $x_0$, so no common constant follows
Nothing: convexity on the open set $\mathbb{R}$ makes the constant equal everywhere
The constant $M-f(x_0)=2x_0+1$ is negative for $x_0<-\tfrac{1}{2}$, so the estimate fails there

questions.question: Let $g(x)=0$ for $x\leq0$ and $g(x)=1$ for $x>0$. Every sublevel set $\{x\in\mathbb{R}\colon g(x)\leq\alpha\}$ is convex, so $g$ is quasi-convex, yet $g$ jumps at the interior point $0$. Why is this consistent with the continuity theorem for convex functions?
options: $0$ is a boundary point of the sublevel set $(-\infty,0]$, and jumps are allowed at boundary points
The jump of $g$ at $0$ goes upwards, and a convex function may jump upwards
$g$ is not convex, and quasi-convexity alone does not force continuity at interior points
The theorem only covers functions on bounded convex sets, and $\mathbb{R}$ is unbounded

questions.question: Let $f(x)=2x^2$ for $x\leq1$ and $f(x)=\alpha x+\beta$ for $x>1$, with $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$. For which pairs $(\alpha,\beta)$ is $f$ convex on $\mathbb{R}$?
options: Exactly those with $\alpha+\beta=2$ and $\alpha\geq4$
Exactly those with $\alpha+\beta=2$
Exactly those with $\alpha\geq4$
Exactly those with $\alpha\leq4$ and $\alpha+\beta=2$

questions.question: Let $f\colon[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ be given by $f(0)=1$ and $f(x)=x$ for $0<x\leq1$. Which statement about convexity and a minimum of $f$ on $[0,1]$ is correct?
options: $f$ is not convex, since a convex function on $[0,1]$ is continuous at both endpoints
$f$ is convex on the compact set $[0,1]$, so it attains a minimum by the extreme value theorem
$f$ is not convex, since its value jumps up at $0$, while a convex function may only jump down
$f$ is convex but has no minimum, as the extreme value theorem needs continuity on $[0,1]$
